title: Why Trump Nixed Execution Livestream
author: Ken Klippenstein

The news media is framing Trump's decision to cancel the
[livestream](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/trump-dons-executioner-hood) of
Nidal Hasan's execution as a Washington story of pure palace intrigue -- Trump
versus Hegseth. This ignores the real story, one that's extraordinary for
several reasons.

First, the decision was never Hegseth's to make; it was the president's alone,
as I [reported](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/trump-dons-executioner-
hood). Second, he initially supported it, [saying
so](https://x.com/cspan/status/2108671065756987581) to a reporter on October
9. Third and most significantly, Trump's reversal is the result of people
power, with an overwhelming majority of Americans -- including his own
supporters -- opposed to the grotesque spectacle worthy of ancient Rome.

Yet instead of a story about ordinary Americans standing up to the most
powerful leader on earth _and winning_ , headline after headline frames it as
a Washington drama, as shown below. Consciously or not, they turn what is
basically a story about people power into just another Trump fuck-up.

See for yourself:

  * NYT: [Hegseth's Plan to Livestream Execution Drew Opposition From Many](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/us/politics/hegseth-livestream-execution-hasan.html)

  * Washington Post: [Trump cancels Hegseth's plan to live-stream Fort Hood shooter's execution](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2026/10/15/trump-cancels-hegseths-plan-live-stream-fort-hood-shooters-execution/)

  * Bloomberg: [Trump rejects Hegseth's bid to stream firing squad execution](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-15/trump-rejects-hegseth-s-bid-to-livestream-firing-squad-execution)

  * NBC News: [White House overrules Pete Hegseth again, this time on livestreaming execution](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/national-security/white-house-overrules-pete-hegseth-time-livestreaming-execution-rcna603735)

The New York Times'
[report](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/15/us/politics/hegseth-livestream-
execution-hasan.html) is the most striking example. It is organized around the
power players it credits with getting the decision reversed. There's a section
on "The General," Lt. Gen. Sean MacFarland, Fort Hood's commander at the time.
Another covers Archbishop Timothy P. Broglio ("The Archbishop"). There's even
a nod to the "dozens of retired admirals and generals and other officers" who
"published an open letter opposing Mr. Hegseth's plan to broadcast the
execution" -- as if anyone gives a shit about a bunch of military brass's
strongly worded letter. And if that weren't comical enough, there's a section
on "Congress," the living embodiment of a strongly worded letter that is the
quintessential return to sender.

What the Times story never mentions is that Americans are united in their
hatred of the idea, as new polling makes clear. They are the real protagonist
of this story -- not Trump, Hegseth, the military brass, or any other big
shots.

An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos [poll](https://abcnews.com/Politics/wide-
majority-americans-oppose-livestreaming-nidal-hasans-
execution/story?id=137263671) released Thursday morning -- hours before Trump
announced the reversal, according to ABC -- found 80 percent of Americans
oppose livestreaming Hasan's execution. Just 18 percent support it. Ninety-one
percent of Democrats oppose the livestream, along with 83 percent of
independents and 64 percent of Republicans. Even MAGA Republicans are against
it, by a 55 percent majority. So are 65 percent of Trump's 2024 voters.

A separate [YouGov](https://thehill.com/policy/defense/6149686-poll-opposes-
liveexecution/) poll asked about broadcasting executions in general. About 7
in 10 Americans opposed it, including Republicans by 52 to 31.

It's not squeamishness about the death penalty. Fifty-three percent of
Americans want Hasan executed by firing squad. But 69 percent of those people
still didn't want it broadcast. The public clearly draws a clear line between
punishment and spectacle.

The Trump-versus-Hegseth framing also ignores that Trump was on board until
the whole country turned on him. Asked on October 9 whether he'd approved the
livestream, he said: "Did I approve? Absolutely." The next day he argued for
it himself: "By showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did."

Far from reining in a rogue defense secretary, this is a story of a president
abandoning a position he personally endorsed just days ago.

Trump all but admits it. His Truth Social post announcing his reversal never
mentions Hegseth. He doesn't mention Congress, the brass or the archbishop
either. The only people he acknowledges are the public: "many very good and
well meaning people would rather not watch him die."

The White House would clearly prefer another explanation. An official told NBC
News that Trump hadn't known Hasan was paralyzed, and that this factored into
the decision. Hasan has used a wheelchair since he was shot during his capture
in 2009. That detail has appeared in coverage of the case all week.

Crediting generals, bishops and senators lets Washington credit Washington,
the perpetual source base of reporting. The 80 percent of Americans who agreed
on something get no section in the Times. And the Washington Post, which co-
sponsored the poll, still put Hegseth in its headline.

Philip K. Dick put it best in a 1978 speech, describing a decency in everyday
people that never makes headlines but holds firm nonetheless:

> "The authentic human being is one of us who instinctively knows what he
> should not do, and, in addition, will balk at doing it. He will refuse to do
> it, even if this brings down dread consequences to him and to those whom he
> loves. This, to me, is the ultimately heroic trait of ordinary people. They
> say 'no' to the tyrant and they calmly take the consequences of this
> resistance. Their deeds may be small, and almost always unnoticed, unmarked
> by history. Their names are not remembered, nor did these authentic humans
> expect their names to be remembered. I see their authenticity in an odd way:
> not in their willingness to perform great heroic deeds but in their quiet
> refusals."
